title: Indian Doctors Validate CRIB-II Score as Key Predictor of Mortality in Premature Newborns
excerpt: A growing body of research from Indian hospitals confirms that the CRIB-II scoring system outperforms other tools in identifying premature neonates at highest risk of in-hospital death, with accuracy rates exceeding 88 percent.
body:
• The CRIB-II scoring system achieved 85–96 percent accuracy in predicting mortality among premature neonates across multiple Indian hospital studies.
  • At a cutoff score of 10 or above, CRIB-II outperformed the Extended Sick Neonatal Score (ESNS) with 96.4 percent specificity versus 71.1 percent.
  • Mortality rose sharply with higher CRIB-II levels — from zero percent at Level I to 100 percent at Level IV in a 140-patient Mumbai study.
  • Researchers say the tool's simplicity makes it especially suited for India's overstretched neonatal intensive care units.

A series of studies from Indian hospitals has established the Clinical Risk Index for Babies-II (CRIB-II) as a reliable, easy-to-use scoring system for predicting in-hospital mortality among premature newborns — a finding with direct implications for how overburdened neonatal intensive care units (NICUs) in India and other developing countries triage their most vulnerable patients.

What the Research Found

The most recent study, published in Indian Pediatrics in May 2025 by researchers at IMS and SUM Hospital in Bhubaneswar, Odisha, compared CRIB-II against the Extended Sick Neonatal Score (ESNS) in 110 preterm neonates born at or before 32 weeks of gestation. CRIB-II scored an area under the ROC curve (AUC) of 0.91, versus 0.85 for ESNS. At a cutoff of 10 or above, CRIB-II achieved a sensitivity of 85.2 percent, specificity of 96.4 percent, and overall predictive accuracy of 93.6 percent — substantially outperforming ESNS on every metric, according to lead author Goolla Akhila and neonatologist Debasish Nanda.

"CRIB II score has a better predictive ability for in-hospital mortality in comparison with ESNS."

— Goolla Akhila et al., IMS and SUM Hospital, Bhubaneswar

A separate prospective study from a tertiary care hospital in Mumbai, published in the Ethiopian Journal of Health Sciences, evaluated 140 preterm neonates between 23 and 32 weeks of gestational age. The results were striking: mortality climbed from zero percent in Level I (scores 1–5) to 3.84 percent in Level II, 64.70 percent in Level III, and 100 percent in Level IV (scores above 15). The CRIB-II score showed a sensitivity of 84.78 percent, specificity of 90.42 percent, and diagnostic accuracy of 88.57 percent.

How CRIB-II Works

Originally developed in 2003 from data on 54 neonatal units in the United Kingdom, the CRIB-II score uses five variables — birth weight, gestational age, sex, body temperature at admission, and base excess from blood gas analysis — to generate a score between 0 and 27. Lower scores indicate better prognosis. Unlike more complex scoring systems such as SNAP-II or SNAPPE-II, which require multiple laboratory parameters and lengthy evaluations, CRIB-II can be calculated within the first hour of a neonate's admission to the NICU.

This simplicity is a decisive advantage in resource-limited settings. As researchers from Government Medical College in Srinagar, Jammu and Kashmir, noted in a separate study published in the International Journal of Contemporary Pediatrics, CRIB-II "with its simplicity, need for uncomplicated variables and minimal time to generate a score" makes it a practical choice for busy NICUs across India.

Why It Matters for India

India accounts for the largest share of preterm births globally. According to the World Health Organization, approximately 3.5 million babies are born prematurely in the country each year, and preterm birth complications remain a leading cause of death in children under five. Many district-level and rural NICUs lack the staffing, equipment, and laboratory access needed to run complex illness-severity assessments within hours of admission.

CRIB-II addresses this gap. By relying on a small set of easily obtainable clinical variables, it allows even understaffed units to quickly stratify risk and direct scarce resources — ventilators, surfactant therapy, specialist nursing — toward the neonates who need them most.

A multicentric Indian study cited in the Bhubaneswar paper found that at a cutoff of 7 or above, CRIB-II had a sensitivity of 83.8 percent and specificity of 57.8 percent, while CRIB-II also showed better predictive accuracy than SNAPPE-II for major morbidities and combined adverse outcomes.

The Diaspora Angle

For Indian-origin physicians and healthcare professionals abroad, the findings reinforce the case for adopting standardized, evidence-based risk tools in NICUs across South Asia. Organizations such as the Indian Academy of Pediatrics and diaspora-led medical NGOs that fund neonatal care in India could use these validated benchmarks to guide equipment purchases and training programs at partner hospitals.

What Comes Next

In a January 2026 commentary in Indian Pediatrics, Aditya Bhatt and Somashekhar Nimbalkar of Pramukhswami Medical College in Gujarat called the Bhubaneswar study a contribution that "strengthens the existing evidence base" and will "inform both future research and bedside decision-making." They noted, however, that performance of scoring tools for predicting long-term neurodevelopmental outcomes — not just survival — remains an open question.

Larger, multicentric trials are needed to validate CRIB-II cutoff values across diverse Indian populations and to assess whether combining it with newer biomarkers could improve its predictive power for morbidity as well as mortality. For now, the consensus from Indian neonatologists is clear: CRIB-II deserves a routine place in every NICU admission workflow.
